entities.name: Keita dynasty
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Keita dynasty was the ruling dynasty of the Mali Empire (c. 1230-1600 CE), one of medieval Africa's greatest empires, which at its height controlled the gold and salt trade across the western Sahara, encompassing modern Mali, Senegal, Gambia, Guinea-Bissau, Guinea, and parts of Mauritania and Niger. The dynasty's most famous ruler, Mansa Musa I (r. 1312-1337 CE), made a 1324-1325 pilgrimage to Mecca that is legendary for the gold he distributed, causing currency devaluation across North Africa and the Middle East.

The dynasty traces its origins to Sundiata Keita, who defeated the Sosso king Sumanguru Kante at the Battle of Kirina (c. 1235 CE), founding the Mali Empire. Sundiata's story is preserved in the Sundiata Epic, an oral tradition still performed by West African griots. The Keita dynasty presided over the construction of Timbuktu as an Islamic scholarly center — Sankore mosque-university became one of the medieval world's great centers of learning with 25,000 students.

Mansa Musa I's 1324 Hajj pilgrimage through Cairo — with a retinue of 60,000 and 80 camels laden with gold — is sometimes cited as the act of the wealthiest individual in history, who spent so much gold in Cairo that it devalued for the next 12 years. His return journey included the capture of Timbuktu and Gao, consolidating Mali's control of trans-Saharan trade.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Keita dynasty's Mali Empire was medieval West Africa's greatest state, and Mansa Musa's legendary gold pilgrimage to Mecca — which devalued currencies across North Africa — remains history's most famous demonstration of African imperial wealth.
